blocks.text: **Traversing** a list means visiting every node once, in order. It's the first step of almost every linked list operation — printing, searching, counting, finding the tail, or reaching position k. In all three types the idea is the same: a pointer `curr` hops from node to node along the arrows. What changes is **which arrows** you follow and **when you stop**.

blocks.alt: How each type of walk ends. Singly: curr follows next arrows and stops when it reaches null. Doubly: curr can walk forward to null, or start at the tail and follow prev arrows back to the null before the head. Circular: there is no null; curr stops when it comes back round to the head.

blocks.text: 1. Singly linked list: follow next until null
Put `curr` on the head and repeat two things: **visit** the node, then **move** with `curr = curr.next`. When `curr` becomes null you've passed the last node. You can only ever go forward.

blocks.caption: curr hops forward one arrow at a time until it falls off the end onto null.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** The same loop, with one change, does everything else: count with a counter, search by returning when `curr.val` matches, or stop one node early (`while (curr.next !== null)`) to land on the **tail**.
2. Doubly linked list: forwards and backwards

Walking forward is the same loop. The difference is that you can also walk **backward**: start at the **tail** and follow `prev` until null. If you only have the head, one forward walk finds the tail first — many implementations simply keep a `tail` pointer alongside `head` so the backward walk can start immediately.

blocks.caption: Walk forward with next, remember the last node, then walk back with prev.

blocks.code:
def walk_both_ways(head):
    forward = []
    curr, tail = head, None
    while curr is not None:        # forward: follow next until None
        forward.append(curr.val)
        tail = curr                # remember the last node we saw
        curr = curr.next
    backward = []
    curr = tail
    while curr is not None:        # backward: follow prev from the tail
        backward.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.prev
    return [forward, backward]

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1)** beyond the output. Being able to walk back is what makes a doubly linked list right for **back** buttons, undo, and finding the k-th node from the end without a second pointer.
3. Circular linked list: stop when you're back at the start

A circular list has **no null**: the last node points back to the head. A `while (curr !== null)` loop would never end. Instead, remember the node you started from and stop when `curr` comes back to it. Use a **do … while** loop so the starting node is visited before the first check — with a plain `while (curr !== head)`, the loop would stop before it starts.

blocks.caption: Visit, move, and stop the moment curr is back at the head.

blocks.code:
def walk_circular(head):
    values = []
    if head is None:
        return values                 # an empty ring has nothing to visit
    curr = head
    while True:
        values.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
        if curr is head:              # stop when we're back at the start
            break
    return values

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** You can start the walk from **any** node — every node is reachable from every other — which is exactly why circular lists suit turn-taking: whoever's turn it is, `curr.next` is the next player.

items: **Using `while (curr !== null)` on a circular list** — it never ends. Compare with the start node instead.
**Moving `head` instead of a copy** — `head = head.next` loses the list. Always walk with a separate `curr`.
**Forgetting the empty list** — in a circular walk, `head.next` on a null head crashes before the loop starts.
**Walking a doubly linked list backward from the head** — the head's prev is null; the backward walk has to start at the **tail**.
**Reading `curr.next` after `curr` became null** — check for null first, then use the node.
Every traversal is **visit, then move**, with a pointer separate from the head.
**Singly**: follow `next` until null. **Doubly**: follow `next` to null, or `prev` from the tail back to null. **Circular**: stop when you're **back at the start**.
Each walk is **O(n) time and O(1) space**; counting, searching and finding the tail are the same loop with a small change.
